s: Quanta Services DEF 14A filed 10 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 26 Mar 2026); NYSE close 21 Aug 2026
m: 707,757 shares beneficially owned x $639.34 close = $452M; holdings basis, excludes proceeds of prior sales
did: Began as a lineman, ran Quanta subsidiary North Houston Pole Line from 2001, became Quanta COO in 2013 and CEO in 2016; grew revenue from $7.6B to over $27B by 2025 by owning the craft labour utilities need for grid, renewables and data-centre work.
why: The scarce input in electrification is not equipment but trained linemen. Austin kept and trained crews through downturns and signed multi-year master service agreements, so when utility capex and data-centre load jumped after 2021 Quanta priced on availability rather than on low bid.
obst: The oil and gas pipeline division Austin had built collapsed with the 2015-16 crude crash and again when Keystone XL was cancelled in 2021; he wrote it down and moved the workforce into electric power and utility-scale solar.
turn: The October 2021 purchase of Blattner Energy for about $2.7B, which made Quanta the largest US utility-scale renewables contractor months before the Inflation Reduction Act passed.

s: Cactus Inc DEF 14A filed 31 Mar 2026 (ownership as of 18 Mar 2026); NYSE close 21 Aug 2026
m: Cactus WH Enterprises holds 9,486,249 CC units jointly controlled by Scott and Joel Bender; half attributed to Joel (4,743,125) plus his own 235,185 Class A = 4,978,310 x $69.43 = $346M The split is an assumption, not a disclosure; SCOTT_BENDER is priced from the same block on the same basis so the two records cannot together exceed the vehicle.
did: Co-founded Cactus Wellhead in Houston in 2011 with his brother Scott, after both ran Wood Group Pressure Control, on the bet that shale operators would rent wellheads and frac valves instead of buying them; served as President through the 2018 IPO and the 2023 FlexSteel pipe acquisition.
why: Renting rather than selling let the same wellhead earn across many wells, and Cactus staffed its own service technicians in the basins instead of using contractors, so it carried the labour cost and kept the margin. That combination held pricing through the 2020 collapse when rivals discounted.
obst: The 2020 price war and pandemic cut the US rig count from about 800 to under 250 and Cactus revenue nearly halved; the brothers kept the service crews on payroll rather than furloughing them and took share when activity returned.
turn: The February 2018 IPO on the NYSE, which turned a seven-year-old private wellhead maker into a listed company and put a public price on the brothers' Cactus WH holding for the first time.

s: Nutex Health DEF 14A filed 13 Mar 2026 (ownership as of 28 Feb 2026); Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,857,879 shares, 32.57% of 5,643,695 outstanding, held via Micro Hospital Holding LLC and the Vo Family LP, x $185.84 close = $345M
did: An anaesthesiologist who from 2010 built Nutex Health, a network of physician-owned micro-hospitals in Texas and eleven other states, and took it public in 2022 through a reverse merger with Clinigence Holdings; he still controls about a third of the shares.
why: A micro-hospital bills as a licensed hospital but costs a fraction of one to build, and physician co-ownership supplied both capital and referrals. The federal No Surprises Act arbitration process, which Nutex learned to run at volume from 2023, converted emergency claims insurers had denied into collectible cash.
obst: Nutex wrote off nearly all the goodwill from its 2022 merger, the shares fell under $1 by 2024 and it faced Nasdaq delisting; a reverse split and the arbitration receipts cycle rebuilt the equity from almost nothing.
turn: The 2025 quarters in which independent dispute resolution awards started settling in cash, lifting revenue and the share price more than tenfold in a year.

s: Solaris Energy Infrastructure DEF 14A 2026 (ownership as of 20 Mar 2026); NYSE close 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,314,883 Class A plus 4,240,315 Class B paired with LLC units = 5,555,198 x $53.28 close = $296M
did: Founded Solaris Oilfield Infrastructure in Houston in 2014 to build mobile sand silos for frac sites, listed it in 2017, then in September 2024 bought Mobile Energy Rentals and turned the company into a lessor of gas turbines powering West Texas data centres.
why: The silo business gave Solaris a rentable, redeployable asset base and a balance sheet built for equipment leasing. Applying the same model to turbines let it sign long-term power contracts with data-centre developers years before utilities could deliver interconnections in ERCOT.
obst: The 2020 frac shutdown idled most of the silo fleet and Solaris shares fell under $6; Zartler kept the fleet rather than scrapping it and used the cash-generative rental model to fund the 2024 power pivot.
turn: The September 2024 Mobile Energy Rentals deal, which repriced Solaris from an oilfield service micro-cap into a power infrastructure company and multiplied the share price several times over.

s: Comfort Systems USA DEF 14A filed 9 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 1 Mar 2026); NYSE close 21 Aug 2026
m: 171,523 shares x $1,655.61 close = $284M; holdings basis, excludes proceeds of prior sales
did: Joined Comfort Systems USA in Houston in October 2003 as a regional vice president and has been chief executive since December 2011; turned a roll-up of local mechanical contractors into the main builder of the cooling and electrical plant inside US chip fabs and data centres.
why: Comfort Systems kept its acquired contractors as independent local operators with their own customer relationships while centralising bonding, insurance and capital. That let it staff several billion-dollar fab and data-centre jobs at once, a scale no single regional mechanical contractor could match.
obst: Lane took over in 2011 with the company still shrinking from the commercial construction bust; he sold off underperforming operating units and rebuilt around industrial and technology customers rather than office buildings.
turn: The 2019 acquisition of Walker Engineering, which took Comfort Systems into large-scale electrical work and opened the semiconductor fab and hyperscale data-centre projects that drove the share price past $1,000.

s: Intuitive Machines DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 10 Apr 2026); Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,176,246 Class A plus 12,342,213 Class C paired one-for-one with LLC units = 13,518,459 x $18.32 close = $248M
did: Left his job as deputy director of NASA Johnson Space Center to co-found Intuitive Machines in Houston in 2013 with Kam Ghaffarian and Tim Crain; as chief executive he landed Odysseus on the Moon in February 2024, the first US soft landing since 1972 and the first ever by a private company.
why: NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme paid fixed-price for delivery rather than cost-plus for development, which suited a small team next door to Johnson that could hire experienced flight controllers and build its own lander instead of subcontracting it.
obst: Odysseus caught a landing leg and tipped over on touchdown in February 2024, cutting the mission short; the follow-up Athena lander also toppled in March 2025, and Altemus had to keep NASA contracts and investors while fixing the landing sensor and geometry.
turn: The February 2023 SPAC merger that listed Intuitive Machines, followed twelve months later by the Odysseus landing, which converted a Houston contractor into the reference name in commercial lunar delivery.

s: Intuitive Machines DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026 (ownership as of 10 Apr 2026); Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026
m: 359,726 Class A plus 8,870,615 Class C paired one-for-one with LLC units = 9,230,341 x $18.32 close = $169M
did: Co-founded Intuitive Machines in 2013 after fourteen years as a NASA guidance and navigation engineer at Johnson Space Center; as chief technology officer he built the precision landing and hazard-avoidance stack that flew Odysseus to the lunar south pole in February 2024.
why: Landing on the Moon is a navigation problem, not a rocket problem, and Crain owned the software rather than buying it. Keeping terrain-relative navigation in-house let Intuitive Machines sell it separately to NASA and other landers while charging for the delivery itself.
obst: A laser rangefinder left disabled before launch nearly ended the IM-1 mission; Crain's team rewrote flight software mid-cruise to substitute an experimental NASA lidar payload as the primary altimeter, which is the only reason Odysseus reached the surface.
turn: The 23 February 2024 landing of Odysseus, which validated the navigation stack in flight and turned a decade of unproven engineering into a bankable product line.

s: Cheniere Energy DEF 14A filed 7 Apr 2026; NYSE American close 21 Aug 2026
m: 724,062 shares held through grantor retained annuity trusts x $277.51 close = $201M; excludes 88,162 unvested RSUs and any prior realized proceeds
did: Took over Cheniere Energy in May 2016, months after the board removed founder Charif Souki, and ran the Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi terminals to become the largest LNG exporter in the world, lifting output past 45 million tonnes a year and paying down roughly $10B of debt.
why: Cheniere sells liquefaction capacity on twenty-year take-or-pay contracts with a fixed fee plus 115 percent of the gas cost, so the margin does not move with commodity prices. Fusco stopped building on spec, contracted trains before sanctioning them and turned the fee stream into a debt-paydown machine.
obst: He inherited a company with about $30B of project debt, no free cash flow and a founder-led culture of building ahead of contracts; the 2020 collapse in LNG demand forced cargo cancellations in the middle of the Corpus Christi build-out.
turn: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which redirected US cargoes to Europe and let Cheniere sign a wave of long-term contracts that funded the Corpus Christi Stage 3 expansion.

s: Targa Resources DEF 14A filed 26 Mar 2026; NYSE close 21 Aug 2026
m: 665,455 shares beneficially owned at the 2026 record date x $299.10 close = $199M
did: Joined Targa Resources in Houston in 2004 as a treasury analyst at age 26, became chief financial officer in 2015 and chief executive in 2020; collapsed the MLP structure, bought in the Badlands and DevCo interests and built out Permian gathering to roughly 30 plants.
why: Midstream value comes from fee-based volume under long-term acreage dedications, not commodity spread. Meloy simplified Targa into a single C-corp, bought back the joint-venture interests that leaked cash flow to partners, and timed plant additions to Permian rig schedules so each filled on start-up.
obst: Targa entered 2020 with heavy leverage and a distribution it could not cover; Meloy cut the dividend by 89 percent within weeks of taking over as CEO, a step the market punished before the deleveraging worked.
turn: The 2022 buy-in of the DevCo joint-venture interests for about $925M, which returned full ownership of the Permian gathering and processing cash flow to Targa shareholders.

s: Sterling Infrastructure DEF 14A filed 25 Mar 2026; Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026
m: 369,839 shares, about 1% of the class, at the 2026 proxy date x $516.81 close = $191M
did: Joined Sterling Construction in The Woodlands in October 2015 when it was a near-insolvent low-bid highway contractor and became chief executive in 2017; rebuilt it as Sterling Infrastructure around e-commerce and data-centre site work, taking the shares from about $4 to over $500.
why: He walked away from lump-sum heavy highway bidding, where the low bidder owns every risk, and bought into e-infrastructure site development, where work is negotiated, margins run three to four times higher and a handful of hyperscale customers repeat. Backlog quality, not backlog size, became the metric.
obst: Sterling had negative equity, a going-concern shadow and a string of loss-making Texas highway contracts when he arrived; he had to work off the legacy jobs while borrowing to buy Tealstone and then Plateau Excavation.
turn: The October 2019 purchase of Plateau Excavation for about $400M, which gave Sterling the Southeast data-centre and distribution-centre site work that now drives most of its profit.

s: Applied Optoelectronics DEF 14A filed 24 Apr 2026; Nasdaq close 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,449,150 shares, 1.8% of the class, at the 2026 record date x $124.82 close = $181M
did: Founded Applied Optoelectronics in Sugar Land in 1997 to make its own laser chips, and has run it ever since; the company now ships 400G and 800G optical transceivers to hyperscale data centres and cable operators, and listed on Nasdaq in 2013.
why: Almost every transceiver rival buys lasers from a third party. Lin kept the gallium arsenide and indium phosphide fabs in Texas and China, so Applied Optoelectronics controlled its own supply and yields when laser capacity was the industry bottleneck for AI cluster interconnect.
obst: Amazon and other hyperscalers cut orders in 2018-19, the shares fell more than 80 percent, and the company took years of losses and a securities class action before the AI build-out revived demand for its 800G parts.
turn: The 2024-25 shift to 800G transceivers for AI clusters, and the strategic investments from Amazon and Nvidia-linked customers, which took the share price from single digits to above $100.

s: Fervo Energy 424B4 IPO prospectus dated 12 May 2026 (ownership as of 29 Apr 2026); NYSE close 21 Aug 2026
m: 6,297,923 Class B shares held plus 1,402,830 exercisable options = 7,700,753 x $16.92 close = $130M; option strikes not deducted
did: A drilling engineer at BHP who quit for business school and co-founded Fervo Energy in Houston in 2017 with Jack Norbeck, applying shale horizontal drilling and fibre-optic sensing to geothermal; Fervo built Project Red in Nevada and the 500MW Cape Station in Utah, and IPO'd in May 2026 raising $1.89B.
why: Geothermal had been limited to rare natural hot-water reservoirs. Horizontal wells with multi-stage stimulation create the permeability instead of finding it, which makes the resource ubiquitous, and each Fervo well drilled faster and cheaper than the last on the same learning curve shale followed after 2010.
obst: Investors treated geothermal as a dead category and drilling costs were the reason; Fervo had to prove the learning curve in public, cutting Cape Station well times from about 70 days to under 20 while pre-selling power to Google and Southern California Edison.
turn: The 2023 Project Red demonstration in Nevada, which delivered continuous power to Google under the first corporate enhanced-geothermal PPA and unlocked the capital for Cape Station.
